passage:
The corridor was empty after the last bell. Neelam, Kiran's friend since Class 6, found Kiran by the water cooler, staring at the floor.
"You didn't say anything in English class today."
"They laughed when I said 'vater'. Everyone did." Kiran's voice cracked. "I'm never speaking again."
"Who laughed? Arjun?"
"All of them. I came from the village school, Neelam. My English is only..."
"Your maths answers are the best in class. And I say 'sheep' like 'ship'. Sit with me at lunch tomorrow. We'll read the lesson aloud together, and you can practise on me."
Kiran wiped an eye. "Just you?"
"And Meera. She's kind."

qa.q: Where did Neelam find Kiran after the last bell?
qa.a: Neelam found Kiran by the water cooler in the empty corridor.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling after being laughed at over the word "vater"?
qa.a: Kiran felt ashamed and hurt. The cracking voice and the vow of never speaking again show how deeply the laughter stung.

qa.q: What small step did Neelam offer to help Kiran speak again?
qa.a: Neelam invited Kiran to sit together at lunch and read the lesson aloud, so Kiran could practise on a friend. It was a low-pressure start with supportive people.

qa.q: What might Neelam want Kiran to know when Neelam admits saying "sheep" like "ship"?
qa.a: Neelam wants Kiran to know that everyone makes mistakes with English and it does not measure ability. Sharing a mistake makes Kiran feel less alone.

grounding: A teenager from a village school is mocked over an English word, stops speaking in class, and a friend offers supportive practice.

passage:
I am Shankar. My school in Vidarbha taught in Marathi and I learnt English from books. In Class 9 in the city school I read aloud once, and a boy imitated the way I said "world". Half the room laughed.
After that I kept my hand down. Even when I knew the answer I felt my throat tighten, and my face got hot. Teachers marked me "quiet".
Then Simran, who sat next to me, said one day, "I also stumble on 'thorough'. Want to make a reading pair? Ten minutes at lunch." We read paragraph after paragraph. By December I put my hand up, shaking a little, and the room was quiet in the good way.

qa.q: Which subject language had Shankar's earlier school in Vidarbha used?
qa.a: Shankar's school in Vidarbha taught in Marathi.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel after the boy imitated the way Shankar said "world"?
qa.a: Shankar felt ashamed and afraid of being laughed at again. The tight throat and hot face show it, and that is why the hand stayed down.

qa.q: What did Simran do that helped Shankar speak up again?
qa.a: Simran admitted stumbling on "thorough" too and suggested a reading pair at lunch. Practising together in private helped Shankar's confidence grow until a hand went up.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Simran to offer the reading pair?
qa.a: Simran may have felt a little shy but kind, sharing a weakness first so Shankar would not feel alone. It took some courage to admit stumbling too.

grounding: A teenager from a vernacular school is mocked for accent, stops speaking in class, and regains confidence with a supportive peer.

passage:
Salma had topped her Urdu-medium school in the kasba, but in the new English-medium school in the district town, the first time she read aloud, she said "wery" for "very". Two boys at the back repeated it in a squeaky voice all week: "Wery good, wery nice."
After that Salma stopped raising her hand. When Sir asked her a question, she stared at the desk and whispered, "I don't know," though she did.
Abhinav, who sat next to her, noticed. One lunch break he said, "My Punjabi aunt says 'sikool'. She's a doctor. Accents are just maps of where you're from."
Salma laughed despite herself.
They started practising the chemistry answers together on the bus stop bench, Salma explaining the science, Abhinav helping with a few words.
Three weeks later, when Sir asked about valency, Salma raised her hand. Her voice shook for the first sentence. Then it didn't.

qa.q: What word did Salma say for "very"?
qa.a: Salma said "wery" for "very".

qa.q: Why did Salma stop raising her hand?
qa.a: Salma felt ashamed and humiliated after the boys mocked her accent all week, so she whispered "I don't know" even when she knew the answer.

qa.q: What made the difference for Salma?
qa.a: A supportive peer, Abhinav, made her laugh about accents and practised with her, which slowly rebuilt her confidence to speak.

qa.q: How does Abhinav see Salma?
qa.a: Abhinav sees her as clever and capable, noticing her silence and treating her accent as just a map of where she's from.

grounding: A teenager from a vernacular school is mocked for her accent and stops speaking, and a supportive peer helps her confidence return.

passage:
Selin had come to the big Istanbul high school on a scholarship from a small town near Konya. In English class, she said "tink" for "think", and a boy at the front repeated it in a heavy voice. Some girls laughed. Someone said her English was "very village".
After that, Selin kept her eyes on her notebook. In group work, she wrote answers for others to say.
Aiko, a Japanese exchange student who also struggled with "th", sat beside her on the ferry one afternoon. "They laugh at me too," Aiko said. "But you write better English than any of them. I read your essay."
Selin shrugged, but her cheeks were pink.
They made a deal: every ferry ride, ten minutes of English, only between them, no laughing except at the seagulls.
In December, Selin read her essay to the class. When the same boy smirked, Aiko began clapping first, loudly.

qa.q: Where did Aiko and Selin practise English?
qa.a: They practised on the ferry, ten minutes every ride.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling after classmates called her English "very village"?
qa.a: Selin felt ashamed and small, keeping her eyes on her notebook and letting others speak her answers.

qa.q: How did Aiko support Selin, and why did it work?
qa.a: Aiko shared her own struggle and praised Selin's essay, then practised with her privately, giving Selin a safe place to speak before the class.

qa.q: What is it like for Aiko to watch Selin being mocked?
qa.a: Aiko feels sympathy and solidarity, being laughed at too, and wants to stand beside Selin.

grounding: A teenager from a small town is mocked for accent as if it marked her class, and confidence returns with a supportive peer.

passage:
At the coaching institute in Kota, Tarun had come from a Hindi-medium school in Jhansi. In the second week, he asked the physics teacher, "Sir, I am having one doubt in this numerical." A group near the window snorted, and one of them whispered, "One doubt, one doubt," in a mocking singsong. For days the phrase followed him in the corridor.
Tarun stopped asking. He copied the board and sat through classes with his questions stuck in his throat. In the hostel mess, he ate alone.
Shreya, from the same batch, sat opposite him one night. "I heard what they said. By the way, 'doubt' is the most useful word in this building. Everyone has them. You just ask yours."
She started meeting him in the library to solve problems. She asked in English; he answered in Hindi; both understood.
A month later, Tarun raised his hand in class again. No one laughed.

qa.q: What did Tarun ask the physics teacher in the second week?
qa.a: Tarun asked, "Sir, I am having one doubt in this numerical."

qa.q: What does Tarun eating alone in the mess suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt ashamed and isolated after the mocking, pulling away from others as well as from asking questions.

qa.q: What would you advise a student in Tarun's place?
qa.a: Find one supportive peer or teacher to practise with, as Tarun did with Shreya, and remember that asking doubts is the point of class, not a weakness.

qa.q: How might Shreya see what happened to Tarun?
qa.a: Shreya likely feels the mocking was unfair and sees Tarun as a capable student, which is why she reaches out and studies with him.

grounding: A teenager from a Hindi-medium school is mocked for English mistakes and stops asking, and a supportive peer helps confidence return.

passage:
Dear Raghav,
You asked why I stopped sending voice notes about my new school in Indore. Truth is, after eight years at our Hindi-medium school back home, I went silent here. For a month I stopped talking in class at all. In the first week I answered a question with "I am knowing the answer, ma'am," and Sameer repeated it in my accent. The back rows laughed. After that I kept my hand down even in maths, which you know I love.
What changed? Two things. That same afternoon Mrs D'Souza kept Sameer back, and the next morning she told the class that nobody laughs at how someone speaks English in her room. And Tanvi from my bench started saying, "Rafiq, you explain it, you got it first." Last week I explained the probability sum on the board. My sentences weren't perfect. Nobody laughed. Two people copied my method.
Say salaam to your Abbu for me.
Rafiq

qa.q: Which sum did Rafiq explain on the board last week?
qa.a: Rafiq explained the probability sum.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling after the back rows laughed?
qa.a: Rafiq felt ashamed and small, and kept a hand down even in maths, a favourite subject.

qa.q: How did Mrs D'Souza and Tanvi help, and what could other classmates do?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza stopped the mocking the same day and Tanvi kept inviting Rafiq to explain; others could listen to the method, not the accent, like the two who copied it.

qa.q: Why might Tanvi have kept saying "Rafiq, you explain it"?
qa.a: Tanvi probably saw that Rafiq understood maths quickly but had gone quiet, and wanted to offer a safe way back into speaking.

grounding: Shows a teenager from a Hindi-medium school mocked for accent who stops speaking in class, and whose confidence returns with a teacher's response and a supportive classmate.
